Build a prep brief for my next meeting: the invite details from my calendar, recent email threads with the attendees, and any related SharePoint documents \u2014 one page, readable in two minutes.
Go through my sent email and Teams messages from this week and pull out every commitment I made \u2014 things I said I\u2019d do. Turn them into a checklist ordered by when each seems due.
Summarize the SharePoint documents that were shared with me or changed recently, and tell me which ones are actually worth opening \u2014 with a one-line reason each. Save me the clicking.
Catch me up on my Teams messages: summarize this week\u2019s active conversations, flag anything waiting on me, and list any decisions that got made while I wasn\u2019t looking.
Give me my morning brief right now: overnight email worth reading, today\u2019s meetings, and the one thing that needs me first. If it\u2019s useful, set it up to run every weekday morning.
Summarize my week from my email and calendar: what I finished, what I left hanging, who\u2019s still waiting on me. Then offer to make this my Friday afternoon ritual.
Open my most recent Figma file and walk me through it: what\u2019s in it, how it\u2019s organized, and the one structural improvement that would make it easier to work in. Honest opinions welcome.
Take a screenshot of my latest Figma design and give me an honest critique: hierarchy, spacing, contrast, and consistency \u2014 ending with the single change that would improve it most.
Turn my most recent Figma design into working HTML and CSS \u2014 a faithful, responsive version I can open in a browser right away. Tell me what you had to guess so I can correct it.
Read the text in my latest Figma file and rewrite it the way a great product writer would: clearer labels, tighter headlines, no jargon. Show me before and after for every change you\u2019d make.
Check my most recent Figma file for consistency: colors, text styles, and spacing values that drift from the rest of the file. Give me a fix list ordered by how visible each issue is.
Read my most recent Figma design, work out the user flow it implies, and generate a FigJam diagram of that flow so we can spot dead ends and missing states together.
Write developer handoff notes for my latest Figma design: components, spacing, colors, and intended behavior, organized screen by screen \u2014 the doc a developer would otherwise ping me for.
Review my most recent Figma design for accessibility: contrast, touch-target size, text size, and color-only signals. Give me a prioritized fix list with the two issues I should fix first.
Turn my latest Figma design into a short walkthrough: screenshot the key screens and write a one-line story for each \u2014 what the user sees, does, and feels \u2014 ready to share with my team.
Summarize what changed across my Figma files this week: new files, active projects, and what seems to be converging or stalling. Then offer to send me this recap every Friday.
Search Jira for everything assigned to me and give me the honest read: what\u2019s urgent, what\u2019s stale, what\u2019s probably done but not closed, and what I should hand back. One list, ranked.

Find my Jira issues that haven\u2019t moved in two weeks, read their comments, and tell me the likely blocker for each \u2014 plus a suggested next step. Distinguish genuinely stuck from just forgotten.
Summarize what my team shipped recently from Jira: what closed, what slipped, and anything that looks stuck \u2014 written so I could paste it straight into standup or a stakeholder update.
Find the Confluence pages my team edited this week and summarize what changed and what\u2019s worth my attention \u2014 with a one-line reason per page, most important first.

Triage my backlog: find the oldest open issues in my projects, group them into fix-now, schedule-later, and close-candidates with a one-line reason each. Propose the changes \u2014 I\u2019ll approve before you touch anything.
Find issues in my projects that look like duplicates or near-duplicates of each other, and propose which to link or close, with your reasoning. Create the links only after I confirm.
Brief me for standup right now: my in-progress issues, what changed overnight, and any blockers with my name on them. If it\u2019s useful, set this up to run every weekday morning.
Summarize this week across my Jira projects: closed, opened, still stuck, and the one risk worth raising. Then offer to send me this digest every Friday afternoon.
Find the deals most at risk of slipping this quarter \u2014 no recent activity, pushed close dates, contacts gone quiet \u2014 and rank them by value, with the single best save-it move for each.
Build me a pipeline dashboard from my HubSpot data: deals by stage, total and weighted value, what changed this past week \u2014 something clean enough to screenshot into my Monday pipeline review.

Find the contacts I\u2019ve gone quiet on \u2014 open deals or warm conversations with no follow-up in two weeks \u2014 and draft a short, personal re-engagement note for each, based on our last exchange.
Pick my biggest open deal and build a one-page brief: history, the people involved, open items, risks, and the suggested next move. The page I should read before I call them.
Find the messy parts of my CRM \u2014 likely duplicate contacts, deals missing amounts or close dates, records with no owner \u2014 and give me a prioritized cleanup list. Fix only what I approve.
Look at my closed deals from this quarter and tell me what the wins had in common, what the losses had in common, and the one thing the pattern says I should do differently.
Give me my pipeline brief right now: what changed since yesterday, what needs action today, what\u2019s newly at risk. If it\u2019s useful, set it up to run every weekday morning.
Summarize my week in HubSpot: deals moved, new contacts, pipeline added and lost, and how my quarter is tracking. Then offer to make this my Friday wrap-up.
Recap my most recent meeting from Granola: the key decisions, the action items with owners, and anything I personally committed to. End with the one follow-up I should do today.
Go through my meetings from this week and pull out every commitment I made out loud \u2014 things I said I\u2019d do. Turn them into a checklist, ordered by how overdue each one already is.
Find the questions that came up in my recent meetings but never got answered, and tell me which ones are probably blocking something right now. Oldest and most consequential first.
Draft the follow-up notes for my last meeting: a short summary, decisions, and an action list with owners \u2014 written so I could send it to the attendees exactly as-is.
Work out who I meet with most, then summarize our last few conversations: what we discussed, what was promised in each direction, and what\u2019s still open between us.

Build a decision log from my last five meetings: each decision, when it was made, and who was in the room \u2014 as a clean document I can keep extending. Flag any decisions that contradict each other.
Find my recurring one-on-ones and summarize how the last few went: themes, action items each way, and anything I promised but haven\u2019t done. Tell me what to raise next time.
Summarize this week\u2019s meetings: decisions, action items, and loose ends \u2014 the five-minute version of my whole week in rooms. Then offer to send me this digest every Friday.
Build my plan for today from my Asana tasks: the three that matter most and why, what can genuinely wait, and one thing I could finish in under fifteen minutes to get moving.
Find my overdue tasks and sort them into still-matters, needs-a-new-date, and honestly-should-be-closed. Propose the date changes and closures \u2014 I\u2019ll approve before you change anything.

Look at my two most active projects and find up to five tasks that haven\u2019t moved in weeks but look like they\u2019re holding other work up. For each, name the likely blocker and the person I\u2019d need to nudge.
Compare everything assigned to me against the working days left this week and tell me honestly whether it fits. If it doesn\u2019t, propose what to move, shrink, or drop.

Find my tasks that have no due date or no description, and propose quick fixes for each \u2014 dates based on the project\u2019s rhythm, descriptions from the task\u2019s context. Apply only what I approve.
Pull everything I completed in Asana over the past week and write it up as a crisp accomplishments list \u2014 the version I\u2019d actually send my manager. Group it by project.
Give me my task brief right now: due today, overdue, and newly assigned to me since yesterday. If it\u2019s useful, set it up to run every weekday morning.
Summarize my week in Asana: completed, slipped, and newly added \u2014 plus whether my load for next week looks sane. Then offer to make this my Friday review ritual.
Look at my Linear issues and give me the honest read: what\u2019s urgent, what\u2019s gone quiet, what\u2019s probably obsolete, and what I should hand back or close. Ranked, with one-line reasons.
Find issues assigned to me that haven\u2019t moved in two weeks, read their comment threads, and tell me the likely blocker for each \u2014 waiting on review, waiting on someone, or just forgotten.
Summarize my team\u2019s recent Linear activity: what shipped, what slipped, what\u2019s stuck in review \u2014 short enough to paste into standup, specific enough to be worth pasting.
Triage my team\u2019s backlog: group the oldest open issues into fix-now, later, and close-candidates with one-line reasons. You propose the updates, I approve, then you make them.
Find issues in my team that look like duplicates or heavy overlaps, and propose which to merge, link, or close \u2014 with your reasoning. Make the changes only after I confirm.
Pick my most active Linear project and give me a pulse check: real progress versus plan, what\u2019s at risk, and the single thing most likely to delay it. Be specific, not diplomatic.
Find the Linear discussions where someone is waiting on my reply \u2014 comments directed at me with no response \u2014 and draft an answer for each that I can approve or edit before you post it.
Brief me on my Linear queue right now: new assignments, things that moved overnight, and blockers with my name on them. If it\u2019s useful, run this every weekday morning.
Summarize the week in my Linear team: closed, opened, carried over, and whether the cycle is on track. Then offer to send me this digest every Friday.
